items: The first lessons in French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Croatian and English were read again, this time for what a native speaker would find stiff or translated. About 150 phrases now say what people actually say: « Ça dépend du temps » and no longer « Cela dépend du temps ». If you had already done one of these lessons, your review shows the new wording.
French stories and dialogues: twelve sentences reworded after the same kind of read.

Know someone who grew up speaking the language you are learning? Settings now has a link to send them. On a page of their own they read the lessons and the texts, write what is wrong or not what people say, and send their corrections back. The content was written by an AI, and no person has checked it yet.
The words speech recognition understood least from you now go to your AI agent with the request for new dialogues and lessons, so those sounds come back in sentences you say.
Spanish first lessons: the name María is spelt with its accent.

Tongue forward or back (First steps, on a computer, in French, German, Dutch, Turkish, Hungarian, Finnish, Danish and Chinese): hold a u or an ou and the app listens to the sound itself and says where your tongue was. It has been tried with synthetic voices only: take it as a hint.
Find a phrase (First steps): type a word in either language and the lesson phrases that hold it are listed, each with a button to hear it. The lessons double as a phrasebook.

Thirty more first lessons in 24 more languages: Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Malay, Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, Serbian, Romanian, Hungarian, Greek, Turkish, Catalan, Galician, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Afrikaans and Esperanto. Sixty in all there now, as in the first eight languages. Each new lesson is a small scene: at the doctor, at the station, an invitation, or a short story.
Find my level by ear (on the welcome card and in Settings): two sentences at each level, at natural speed, typed from the ear. It says where it gets hard, so you start there instead of guessing.

A record for each sound: every time you say a word on its own in First steps, or pick one of two words one sound apart by ear, it is counted. Progress shows how often speech recognition understood you and which sounds it understands least.

Corrections after a slower, closer second read of the French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Croatian and English texts: five grammar notes, four meanings, and four sentences made more natural.
Just listen now also plays the first lessons you have done, so there is something to follow by ear from the first day. The lessons are listed ten at a time.

Thirty more first lessons in French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Croatian and English, sixty in all there. Each new lesson is a small scene: a visit to the doctor, a problem at the hotel, an invitation, or a story such as the lost bag.

Speaking, on a computer: after you say a line you see about how long you took beside how long the model voice takes, and your long pauses. In Chinese, Thai and Vietnamese, a word said on its own gets a drawing of how your pitch moved.

First lessons from your own AI agent: with AI cowork connected and your level at A1, your agent writes the next lessons when few are left to do, also for a language the app has no lessons for. You approve them before they are added.
Sounds apart (First steps, 24 languages): pairs of words that differ by one sound. You hear one and choose which it was; then you say one and see which of the two your browser heard.

First steps is half as long again: thirty lessons and 240 phrases in each of the 44 languages. The ten new lessons go shopping for clothes, to a restaurant and around town, and talk about free time, people, reasons and rules, and the seasons. Two of them are each a small story to hear, write and say.
Numbers by ear (First steps): your device's voice says a number at natural speed and you type it in digits. Four ranges, up to 10,000, in every language your device has a voice for.
Sounds to notice for every language: 25 more lists, from English and Russian to Arabic, Hindi, Thai, Japanese and Korean. Each sound has a word to hear and to say.

Speaking: when speech recognition hears another word in place of yours, it shows the two side by side with the letters that differ marked. In First steps you can now say each "sound to notice" and see whether you were understood, or what was heard instead.
Read aloud: any story, and any text of your own, can now be practised aloud sentence by sentence from the Library, with the same word-by-word marks as in a sitting.

Twelve stories and dialogues instead of six in 32 languages, from Russian and Turkish to Hindi, Swahili and Thai. The six new ones are a family, a town, a grandmother's birthday, a lost wallet, buying a ticket at the station and a visit to the doctor, from A1 to B1. Every one of the 44 languages now has at least twelve texts.
Corrections after a second read of all 644 stories and dialogues: about forty small fixes, among them notes on lines that a man and a woman say differently.

After a sitting, the small AI model in your browser (where it has one for your language) reads your retelling and suggests corrections a few seconds later. It misses things and is sometimes wrong, so each suggestion is yours to keep for review or to leave.

Write me a story: where your browser has its own small AI model (Chrome on a computer, for French, Spanish, German, English and Japanese), the Library can add a new short text at your level in a few seconds, written on your device around the words you are reviewing. It is a small model: expect about one slip a text. Nothing leaves your device.

First steps doubled again: twenty lessons and 160 phrases in each of the 44 languages. The ten new lessons take you to a market, home, a journey, yesterday, plans, feeling well and unwell, describing things, work, the telephone, and asking for help.

Stories and dialogues in 32 more languages. Every one of the 44 languages now has texts to listen to, read, take dictation from and retell, from Polish, Russian and Turkish to Arabic, Hindi, Vietnamese and Thai. The new sets are a first handful: four stories and two dialogues, at A1 and A2.

Speaking: a word the speech recognition only had as its second guess is now marked as nearly right, not as missed, and it tells you how sure it was of what it heard. Progress now also names the level your speaking supports, beside reading and listening.
Share a text as a link (Library): a teacher can hand out a text to a class, or you can send one to a friend. Whoever opens the link sees the text and adds it to their own library with one tap.

Fairer marking in Arabic, Persian and Urdu: vowel marks and the different shapes of the same letter no longer count against you, and a Persian word is right whether you type it joined up, with a space or with its half-space.

Every word of the texts in 31 languages has been checked against a spelling dictionary, and the new texts were read by a second AI model. A handful of phrases were corrected. No native speaker has read them yet.
Reading looks tidier: a full stop or a comma no longer slips to the start of the next line, and a short word like "J’" stays with the word it belongs to.

First steps: new to a language? Ten short lessons, from everyday phrases to first sentences, starting from nothing, in 44 languages. You hear each phrase, write it and say it, and it then comes back in your review. Choose level A1 to see them first, or open them from the Library.

Letters and sounds: a chart of the letters to hear and practise for Japanese, Korean, Russian, Greek, Arabic, Hindi, Thai and seven more scripts, and a list of the sounds that surprise for nineteen languages, from French and Spanish to Polish, Turkish and Vietnamese.
Record yourself when you speak, and hear your own take after the model's.

With a teacher: send a sitting to a teacher or tutor as a link (Progress). They open it in any browser, write their corrections and send you a link back; opening it puts the corrections beside your sitting and into your review. You can also type corrections in by hand (Words).
LanguageLab installs like an app (Settings), and after one visit it opens without a connection.
Stories written by your AI agent now bring two sentences to write back from their meaning, like the ones that come with the app.
Speaking now listens until you have finished: a pause at a comma no longer cuts you off, and a number you say counts even when the browser writes it in digits.
Conversation on your device: corrections now come from a second pass that looks only for mistakes. They are offered with "Keep for review", because the browser's small model is sometimes wrong.

Twelve languages now come with stories: French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Croatian and English, and smaller sets for Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Swedish. Any other language works with your own texts and with stories from AI cowork. Pick yours in Settings.
A sitting now asks you three questions after you have only heard the story, so you can see how much you follow by ear.
Speak: dialogues you play a part in. You read your lines aloud, then say them from memory.
Conversation: talk with an AI partner who answers and corrects you as you go. It runs on your device where the browser has its own AI model, and otherwise through your AI cowork folder.

Write it back: a sitting shows you what a sentence means and you write it in the language you are learning. It is marked word by word, and works in every browser for the stories that come with the app.
Grammar you have met: each text ends with one point to notice, and the Words screen keeps them all.
Pen pal: write a letter and an AI pen pal answers at your level and corrects you (through the AI cowork folder). Your corrected mistakes come back in review until you get them right.
Just listen plays stories one after another, and Read lets you read anything in your library with a tap for each new word. Both count as input.
Tap a word that has no meaning and, in Chrome or Edge on a computer, it is translated on your device. You can also translate the whole sentence, type your own meaning, or look the word up.
Progress now says which level your numbers support for reading and for listening, with a table level by level.
A Words screen: search your words, fix a meaning, say "I know this", or send a known word back to review.
Bring your own recording: add a podcast or video sound file with its subtitle file, and take dictation from the real voices.
More French: fourteen new stories up to C1, and fourteen dialogues up to B2.
Say it: after the dictation you read three sentences aloud, and the score is the share of your words that speech recognition understood (in browsers that have it).
Twelve more French stories, from A1 to B2. Today now offers the unread story closest to your level.
Progress draws your dictation scores sitting by sitting, and shows how well you were understood when reading aloud.
Leaving a sitting half way now warns you first, and keeps what you typed.
Colour themes: the shared list is in Settings, under Appearance.
Google sign-in is shared with the other apps, so you are not asked to pick your account again.

First version. A sitting takes one French story through four steps: listen without the text, read it and tap the words you don't know, take dictation at natural speed, then retell it in your own words.
The words you tap come back for review inside the sentence you met them in, and you type them.
Progress shows what you can do (words caught by ear, words understood, words produced from memory), with no points and no streak.
With an AI cowork folder, an agent writes new stories at your level and gives each sitting an honest grade.
